newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-FTC, seeking to warn consumers, sues Exxon.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-FTC, seeking to warn consumers, sues Exxon.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC), seeking to warn consumers against paying extra for premium gasoline, sued Exxon Corp on Tuesday for making false advertising claims.
Exxon is the fourth major U.S. oil company to run afoul of the FTC for making overblown claims for its premium gasoline but the first not to settle before a suit was filed.
"We think it is important to bring a lawsuit like this to help educate consumers," said Joel Winston, the FTC's assistant director of advertising practices.
An Exxon spokesman said Tuesday that the company will contest the FTC charge.

The suit will be heard by a federal administrative judge who, if Exxon cannot substantiate its advertising claims with scientific evidence, can order the company to ensure its advertisments are truthful or face financial penalties.
"For years there has been a widespread misconception that for an extra 15 to 20 cents a gallon your engine is going to run cleaner, you are going to get better mileage etc," said Winston of the FTC.
"But for most cars -- except for high-performance sports car types -- the extra benefits are simply non-existant. Premium gasoline doesn't do anything but cost you money," he added.
For its part, Exxon is facing intense pressure to maintain retailing profits and is likely to have an incentive to fight the case, analysts said.

"Competition among oil companies is intense and marketing is under considerable pressure, particularly in the last quarter, as they have not been able to pass on the higher cost of oil," said Holly Gustafson, an industry analyst at County NatWest Securities in Baltimore.
This places increased emphasis on those premium, high-profit products such as Exxon's 93 Supreme gasoline which came under the FTC's scrutiny, to produce the margins.

"I suspect that it is going to go on and on and I am concerned that the penaltis are not sufficient to make them stop it," said David Van Sickle, director of automobile consumer information at the American Automobile Association in Washington.

"Premium gasoline is enormously profitable for the oil companies. It costs an extra nickle to make premium above regular and sell it at 17 cents (a gallon) above. The economics are clear," said Van Sickle.

Meanwhile, if it lost the suit against the FTC and was found to be still making false claims, the maximum fine Exxon would face is $10,000 a day for each infringement, which Winston of the FTC acknowledges is a pretty small dent in the company's 1995 revenues of $124 billion.
"Maybe that's one of the reasons they decided not to enter into a settlement (but) there is only so much we can do," said Winston of the FTC.
